title: India on track for record 50 GW solar year as ALMM-II mandate reshapes domestic supply chain
gist: India will exceed 50 GWdc of solar additions in 2026, a record, but the same ALMM-II local-cell mandate that pulled installations forward has created a cell shortage that lifts utility-scale system prices about 20% by Q4 2026 with only a 3% decline through Q4 2027. Cell output of 29 GW in 2027 still falls 21 GW short of 50 GW annual module demand, and import dependency has shifted from China to Indonesia rather than disappearing — with ALMM-III extending the mandate to wafers in June 2028.

themes.theme: Record installations pulled forward by policy deadline

insights.claim: India added 34 GWdc of solar capacity in H1 2026, 38% above H1 2025, as developers raced to commission projects before the June ALMM-II deadline — meaning the record is a pull-forward of demand, not organic acceleration.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Treat H1 2026 Indian solar volumes as borrowed from H2; module and EPC order books should be expected to air-pocket after the deadline.
insights.quote: India added 34 GWdc of solar capacity in the first half of 2026, 38% above H1 2025 levels, as developers raced to commission projects ahead of the June deadline
insights.locator: India is set to commission more solar capacity in 2026

insights.claim: Full-year 2026 Indian solar additions are forecast to exceed 50 GWdc, surpassing the previous record of 49 GWdc set in 2025 — a record year that is nonetheless only marginally above the prior peak despite a 38% first-half surge.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The gap between a 38% H1 gain and a barely-above-record full year quantifies how sharp the expected H2 slowdown is.
insights.quote: Full-year additions are forecast to exceed 50 GWdc, surpassing the previous record of 49 GWdc set in 2025
insights.locator: India is set to commission more solar capacity in 2026

insights.claim: The phased removal of inter-state transmission charge waivers — cut from 75% to 50% for projects commissioned from July 2026 and set to disappear entirely after July 2028 — was a second, independent driver of the commissioning rush alongside ALMM-II.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A second deadline in July 2028 sets up another pull-forward cycle; project economics for post-2028 commissioning carry a structural cost step-up.
insights.quote: the phased removal of waivers for inter-state transmission charges, which fell from 75% to 50% for projects commissioned from July 2026 onwards and are set to be phased out entirely after July 2028
insights.locator: Installations surge ahead of ALMM-II deadline

insights.claim: H2 2026 momentum is expected to slow on cell capacity constraints and rising module prices, though ALMM-II waivers for net metering and open access projects until 31 December 2026 and the MNRE's July 2026 exemption for projects near completion provide upside.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Exemption carve-outs are the swing factor for H2 volumes — watch the 31 December 2026 waiver expiry as the next demand cliff.
insights.locator: Installations surge ahead of ALMM-II deadline, but slowdown follows

insights.claim: The ALMM-II mandate requiring modules made from domestically manufactured cells in government-supported projects is causing utility-scale solar system prices in India to rise about 20% by Q4 2026, because Indian cell manufacturing has not kept pace with module capacity.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Local-content policy is inflationary before it is deflationary — a 20% system price rise compresses developer IRRs and raises tariffs on new Indian solar PPAs.
insights.quote: India's ALMM-II mandate is a bold step toward building a fully integrated domestic solar supply chain, but cell manufacturing capacity has simply not kept pace with modules,
insights.locator: New Wood Mackenzie research finds utility-scale system prices

insights.claim: Indian cell production is projected at 29 GW in 2027, still 21 GW short of average annual module demand of 50 GW, so the shortage persists through 2027 even as new capacity comes online.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A 21 GW structural cell deficit in 2027 means import reliance and elevated prices are locked in for at least two more years — bullish for non-Chinese cell suppliers into India.
insights.quote: Cell production is projected to reach 29 GW next year, still falling 21 GW short of the average annual module demand of 50 GW.

insights.claim: Indian system prices are forecast to fall only 3% between Q4 2026 and Q4 2027, effectively locking in the 20% price step-up for a full year rather than reversing it.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Developers signing 2027-delivery PPAs at pre-shock tariff assumptions face a margin squeeze; the cost relief only arrives from 2029.
insights.quote: As a result, system prices are forecast to decline by just 3% between Q4 2026 and Q4 2027.

insights.claim: Reaching the expected 130 GW of additional Indian cell capacity by 2029 requires a 49% compound annual growth rate from the 2026 full-build baseline of 88 GW, an execution bar that has to be cleared for prices to stabilise.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A 49% CAGR build-out requirement is the quantified execution risk; slippage extends the price premium beyond 2029.
insights.quote: 130 GW of additional cell capacity is expected to come online by 2029, requiring a compound annual growth rate of 49% from the 2026 full-build baseline of 88 GW.
insights.locator: Import dependency shifts rather than disappears

insights.claim: Any delay to the 14 GW of Indian cell manufacturing capacity currently under construction risks deepening import reliance and driving prices beyond current estimates, making that near-term tranche the single most watchable variable.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Track commissioning of the 14 GW under construction as the leading indicator for whether the 20% price shock persists or worsens.
insights.quote: Any delay to the 14 GW of new cell manufacturing capacity currently under construction risks deepening import reliance and driving prices beyond current estimates.
insights.locator: Import dependency shifts rather than disappears

insights.claim: ALMM-II reduced India's direct cell imports from China but sourcing pivoted to Southeast Asia rather than to domestic supply, with Indonesian cell imports nearly tripling in early 2026.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Local-content mandates relocate the import bill instead of eliminating it — Indonesian cell exporters are the immediate beneficiary of Indian policy.
insights.quote: While ALMM-II has reduced India's direct cell imports from China, sourcing has pivoted toward Southeast Asia, with Indonesian cell imports nearly tripling in early 2026.
insights.locator: Import dependency shifts rather than disappears

insights.claim: India imported 5 GW of wafers and 20 GW of cells in the first five months of 2026, with wafer imports climbing 86% year-on-year to feed domestic cell production — evidence the localisation has moved one step up the chain, not completed it.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The 86% wafer import surge is the measurable signature of mandate-driven supply-chain migration and the reason ALMM-III targets wafers next.
insights.quote: In the first five months of 2026, India imported 5 GW of wafers and 20 GW of cells, with wafer imports climbing 86% year-on-year to support domestic cell production.
insights.locator: Import dependency shifts rather than disappears

insights.claim: India's 20% basic customs duty on imported cells and modules, plus the DGTR's September 2025 recommendation of anti-dumping duties of up to 30% on Chinese-origin solar cells and modules still awaiting a final government decision, is what makes Indonesian-origin supply the attractive alternative.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The pending anti-dumping decision is a binary policy catalyst; a final ruling at up to 30% would further entrench Southeast Asian routing.
insights.quote: in September 2025 the DGTR recommended additional anti-dumping duties of up to 30% on Chinese-origin solar cells and modules, pending a final decision from Central Government
insights.locator: Import dependency shifts rather than disappears

insights.claim: Circumvention scrutiny is likely to follow the Indonesian import surge given the pattern of Chinese cell rerouting already observed in other markets, putting the current Indonesian supply channel at policy risk.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The Indonesian workaround has a limited shelf life; an anti-circumvention case would re-tighten Indian cell supply and re-inflate prices.
insights.quote: though circumvention scrutiny may follow given the pattern of Chinese cell rerouting observed in other markets
insights.locator: Import dependency shifts rather than disappears

insights.claim: The MNRE plans to implement ALMM-III in June 2028 extending the domestic content mandate to solar wafers, signalling India's localisation ambitions run well beyond cells.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A repeat of the 2026 cell squeeze is pre-scheduled for wafers in 2028; wafer capacity build-out in India is the next investment window.
insights.quote: The MNRE's plan to implement ALMM-III in June 2028, extending the mandate to solar wafers, signals that India's domestic content ambitions are far from complete.

insights.claim: ALMM-II is expected to repeat ALMM-I's pattern of multiple exemptions, though with more contained impact because suppliers, developers and policymakers are better prepared this time.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Assume mandate slippage as the base case in Indian solar policy forecasting; exemptions cap both the price upside and the localisation benefit.
insights.quote: The rollout of ALMM-II may follow ALMM-I's pattern of multiple exemptions, though the impact should be more contained given greater preparedness among suppliers, developers and policymakers.

insights.claim: Price stabilisation in Indian solar is conditioned on policy consistency and timely manufacturer execution rather than on capacity announcements alone, making follow-through the real variable through 2029.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Discount announced Indian cell capacity pipelines; only commissioned capacity relieves the price premium.
insights.quote: Prices are expected to stabilise through 2029 as additional cell capacity comes online, but the transition will require policy consistency and timely execution by manufacturers,
